title: Insurance Pays for Accidents; Surety Pays for Broken Promises
summary: Insurance and surety look alike on a contract schedule, but they do opposite jobs. Insurance pools accidental losses and expects to pay claims; a surety bond guarantees that a contractor keeps its promises and expects to be repaid by that contractor. Knowing which one you are holding tells you what it will and will not do when something goes wrong.
body:
Insurance pays for accidents and expects to pay claims. A surety bond guarantees a contractor's promise and expects never to lose money, because the contractor must repay it. Treat them as the same thing and you will call the wrong one on the worst day of the project.

Recall

Q. What does contra proferentem mean?

A. A genuinely ambiguous clause is read against the party that proposed or relies on it. It is one reason risk clauses must be drafted plainly.

Q. In Week 77, what is the main family of international standard contract forms, and what do its colours mean?

A. FIDIC. Broadly, the Red Book is for construction designed by the employer, the Yellow Book for plant and design-build, and the Silver Book for engineer-procure-construct turnkey work with more risk on the contractor.

Q. In Week 71, what is an offering document for?

A. It discloses to investors the facts, risks, terms and use of funds of an investment, so they can decide on full information. It is also the document against which any later misrepresentation claim is measured.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week was about who pays when something goes wrong. Insurance and surety are how you make sure the party that is supposed to pay actually can. A contract can place a risk perfectly and still leave you with nothing, if the party carrying it has no money and no policy behind it. This week Marco joins me, because the owner's project manager is the person who checks, every month, that the insurance and the bonds are still really there.

Insurance: pooling accidents

In plain English: many people pay a small certain amount so that the unlucky few are paid when an accident happens.

The professional framing is risk pooling. An insurer collects premiums from many policyholders, expects a predictable share of them to suffer losses, and pays those losses from the pool. It expects to pay claims; that is its business. On a construction project the core policies are these.

  • Builder's risk, also called course of construction or contractors' all risks: property insurance on the works themselves while they are being built, covering physical loss or damage such as fire, storm or theft, subject to exclusions.
  • Commercial general liability: insurance against claims by third parties for bodily injury or property damage caused by the works or the firm's operations.
  • Professional indemnity, sometimes called errors and omissions: insurance against claims that a designer or consultant was negligent in its professional work.
  • Workers' compensation or employer's liability, depending on the place, for injury to the firm's own workers.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A fire during construction destroys 2,000,000 dollars of completed work. The builder's risk policy has a 50,000 dollar deductible, the amount the insured pays before the policy responds. The insurer pays 1,950,000 dollars to rebuild. The policy may also pay some extra costs, such as debris removal, if it includes that cover. It will usually not pay the owner's lost rent from the resulting delay unless the policy includes delay in start-up cover, often called soft cost or delay cover, which is a separate, negotiated extension. Insurance pays for what its wording describes, and only that.

Surety: guaranteeing a promise

In plain English: a surety company promises the owner that the contractor will do what it agreed, and if the contractor fails, the surety steps in, then chases the contractor for every dollar.

The professional framing is a three-party credit instrument. The principal is the contractor, whose promise is guaranteed. The obligee is the owner, who benefits. The surety is the company that guarantees. Before issuing a bond, the surety underwrites the contractor's finances, management and track record, and takes a written indemnity from the contractor, and often from its owners personally, to repay any loss. A surety expects, in principle, to lose nothing. That is the decisive difference from insurance: surety is closer to a line of credit extended to the contractor than to a pool of accidents.

The main construction bonds are three. A bid bond guarantees that a winning bidder will sign the contract and provide the other bonds. A performance bond guarantees completion of the work, up to a stated maximum called the penal sum. A payment bond, sometimes called a labour and material bond, guarantees that subcontractors and suppliers are paid, which reduces liens on the owner's property. Penal sums, often a percentage of the contract, are commercial practice and sometimes set by public procurement rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

Insurance expects to pay. Surety expects to be repaid. They are not the same promise.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A contractor on a 10,000,000 dollar contract fails halfway through. A performance bond has a penal sum of 50 percent, 5,000,000 dollars. The owner has paid 5,000,000 dollars, and a replacement contractor wants 8,000,000 dollars to finish, against an unpaid contract balance of 5,000,000 dollars. The extra cost is 3,000,000 dollars. The surety's options typically include financing the original contractor to finish, bringing in a replacement, or paying the owner's extra cost up to the penal sum; the bond wording decides which. Here 3,000,000 dollars is within the 5,000,000 dollar penal sum, so the surety's obligation can cover it. Then the surety turns to its indemnity and pursues the contractor and its owners. The owner never has to.

Letters of credit and the two other ideas this week

A letter of credit is a bank's undertaking to pay the owner on presentation of stated documents, often just a written demand. It is fast and certain, which owners like, but it ties up the contractor's bank credit, which the contractor prices into its bid, and it pays a fixed sum without the surety's work of completing the job. This week also covers waiver of subrogation, which stops an insurer who has paid a claim from suing other parties on the same project, and wrap-up programmes, owner- or contractor-controlled insurance covering everyone on site under one set of policies. Those come later in the week.

How the best do it

Well-run owners keep an insurance and bond register from the first contract award: every policy and bond, its insurer or surety, limits, deductibles, named insureds, expiry date and the date the actual wording was reviewed. The project manager checks the register monthly against the contracts, and nobody is allowed on site whose cover has lapsed. A small developer can copy this with one spreadsheet and a monthly diary entry. The register turns insurance from a file of certificates into a control.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: whether premiums and bond costs are deducted or added to the cost of the asset, and how insurance proceeds are treated, depends on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: policies and bonds are what make a risk allocation collectable. Banking: lenders specify required cover and usually want to be named as loss payee or additional insured. Governance: one named person owns the insurance and bond register. Estate: a surety's indemnity signed personally by a contractor's owners reaches their estates; know what you sign if you ever give one. Exit: a buyer will ask which warranties, latent-defect covers and completed-operations covers survive completion.

Professional sign-off required: insurance broker, on the programme; lawyer, on the insurance and bond clauses.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming a policy or bond covers a loss because a certificate says the policy exists. Certificates describe; wordings decide. The control is to read the actual wording for exclusions and conditions, and to keep a register that is checked every month.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner calls the insurer when the contractor goes broke and the surety when a storm floods the basement. Know before you sign which instrument responds to which event.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Roman taught that a lender calls the developer's personal guarantees when the loan goes out of balance. A surety bond is the same idea pointed at the contractor: a guarantee, backed by an indemnity, that lets the owner collect from someone whose business is standing behind other people's promises.

Recap

Insurance pools accidental losses and pays what the wording covers. Surety guarantees a contractor's promise and is repaid by the contractor. Builder's risk, liability, professional indemnity and workers' cover are the core policies; bid, performance and payment bonds are the core bonds; a letter of credit is a bank's cash promise. Keep them in a register and read the wordings.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of the policy that did not respond.
checklist: I can say for each likely loss whether insurance, a bond or a letter of credit responds.
I have read the actual policy wordings, not just the certificates.
I know the deductible on every policy and who pays it.
I know whether delay in start-up cover is included or must be bought separately.
I know the penal sum of every performance and payment bond.
I keep an insurance and bond register with limits, named insureds and expiry dates.
One named person checks the register against the contracts every month.
head: Field checklist
speak: Insurance and surety look alike on a schedule, but they do opposite jobs. Insurance pools accidents. An insurer expects to pay claims, and pays what its wording covers, less the deductible. Builder's risk covers the works themselves, general liability covers third-party claims, professional indemnity covers design negligence. A surety bond guarantees a contractor's promise. It has three parties: the contractor, the owner and the surety, which underwrites the contractor and takes an indemnity so it is repaid if it pays out. Bid bonds guarantee the winner signs, performance bonds guarantee completion up to the penal sum, payment bonds protect subcontractors. A letter of credit is a bank's cash promise, fast but blunt. So I know before I sign which instrument answers which event, I read the wordings, not the certificates, and I keep a register that someone checks every month.
terms: Builder's risk insurance — property insurance on the works while under construction, covering physical loss or damage subject to its exclusions.
Surety bond — a three-party guarantee in which a surety promises the owner that the contractor will perform, backed by the contractor's indemnity to the surety.
Letter of credit — a bank's undertaking to pay a stated sum on presentation of specified documents, often a simple demand.

hostile.q: You have a certificate of insurance from the contractor. Are you sure you are covered for a fire on site?
hostile.a: A certificate tells me a policy exists; it does not tell me what it covers. I have the actual builder's risk wording on file, I know the deductible, the exclusions and that we and the lender are named, and I know whether delay cover is included. The register shows the expiry date and when we last checked it. If any of that is missing for a policy, I treat that cover as unconfirmed until it is fixed.

title: The Policy That Did Not Respond
summary: A composite case: a pipe joint failed on an upper floor over a weekend and flooded five floors of nearly finished fit-out. The builder's risk policy had a water sublimit, did not name the owner, carried no delay cover and had no waiver of subrogation. Seven forensic steps show how a fully insured project still lost months and millions.
body:
This is a composite example. A project that everybody believed was fully insured lost months and millions after one pipe joint failed, because nobody had read what the policy actually said.

Recall

Q. What is the decisive difference between insurance and surety?

A. Insurance pools accidents and expects to pay claims. Surety guarantees a contractor's promise and expects to be repaid by the contractor under its indemnity.

Q. In Week 77, what is a time bar, and why does it matter for insurance claims too?

A. A clause cutting off a claim if notice is late. Insurance policies carry their own notice conditions, so the same discipline of prompt, written notice applies to insurers.

Q. In Week 71, what does a sponsor owe investors when something goes wrong?

A. Prompt, honest and complete disclosure of the problem and its likely effect, consistent with the offering document and any fiduciary or contractual duties. Bad news delayed is usually bad news made worse.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me today because the cost of this failure was measured in two currencies: the repair the insurer argued about, and the interest and lost rent nobody had insured at all. No fact in this story is exotic. The numbers are hypothetical round figures, and the story is assembled from patterns that recur on real projects.

1. Timeline

An owner builds a 40,000,000 dollar residential building under a lump-sum contract. The contract requires the contractor to carry builder's risk insurance for the full value of the works. At award, the contractor provides a one-page certificate of insurance. Nobody asks for the wording. In month 20, with interior finishes complete on most floors, a pressurised water line fails at a joint on the ninth floor on a Friday night. Water runs for two days. On Monday, five floors of finished work are damaged: about 3,000,000 dollars of repair. The contractor claims under its policy. The insurer reserves its rights, then pays a reduced amount. Repairs start in month 25. Opening slips by five months.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Accepting the contractor's certificate at award without reviewing the policy wording. Deciding not to buy owner's delay in start-up cover, to save premium. And signing a contract with no requirement for a waiver of subrogation between the parties on site.

3. Assumptions

The owner assumed that a policy for the full value of the works would pay any loss up to that value. In fact, the wording carried a sublimit for water damage of 500,000 dollars per occurrence, a lower internal limit that applies to one type of loss regardless of the headline limit. The owner assumed it was covered by the contractor's policy. It was not named as an insured, so it had no direct right to claim or to see the insurer's correspondence. And the owner assumed its own losses from delay, interest and lost rent, were part of any insured loss. They were not covered at all.

4. Incentives

The contractor bought the cheapest policy that met the words of the contract, because insurance is a cost in a competitive bid and the contract specified only the limit. The broker placed what the client asked for. The insurer, once the loss arrived, applied its wording exactly, as it was entitled to. The owner's team wanted to keep costs down and saw insurance as paperwork. Each party behaved rationally. Nobody was paid to check that the cover matched the risk.

Say that out loud now.

A certificate tells me a policy exists. Only the wording tells me what it pays.

5. Warning signs ignored

The certificate referred to the policy for terms and conditions, a standard line that should send any reader to the wording. The contractor's insurance schedule in the tender showed a premium far below the other bidders' for the same headline limit. The site had no water-detection or automatic shut-off on the temporary water system, and no weekend watch on floors with live pressure. And the owner's lender had asked, in its commitment letter, to be named on the builder's risk policy; nobody followed up.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment the water started running unseen on a Friday. Up to then, every gap could have been closed: the wording reviewed and the sublimit raised, the owner and lender added as named insureds, delay cover bought, a waiver of subrogation added and a leak-detection system installed. After that weekend, only the claim was left.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the failed joint. Joints fail. It was an owner that treated insurance as a document to collect rather than a promise to read, and so accepted a programme whose wording did not match the risks the contract had allocated.

Roman's view: how the loss was really shared

Roman follows the money. Of the 3,000,000 dollars of repair, the insurer paid the 500,000 dollar water sublimit, less a 100,000 dollar deductible: 400,000 dollars. The insurer then pursued the plumbing subcontractor whose joint failed, through subrogation, its right to step into the insured's shoes and sue whoever caused the loss. That made the subcontractor, the contractor and the owner adversaries while repairs were needed. The subcontractor's own liability insurer pointed to an exclusion for its own defective work. The contractor, holding a 2,600,000 dollar shortfall, claimed the owner had ordered acceleration that caused the failure. Repairs waited while the parties argued.

Then the owner's uninsured costs. Five months of delay at a carrying cost of about 8,000 dollars a day, the figure from Week 78's model, is roughly 1,200,000 dollars of interest, fees and lost net rent. None of it was insured. The contract's liquidated damages did not help, because the contractor argued the delay was caused by an insured event and claimed an extension of time under the contract's own terms.

Now the second worked example, hypothetical: what the prevention would have cost. An owner's broker reviewing the wording at award, perhaps 10,000 dollars of fees. Raising the water sublimit to the full value of the works, a modest addition to the premium. Delay in start-up cover for 12 months of lost net rent and interest, perhaps 60,000 to 100,000 dollars, a market price that varies widely. A waiver of subrogation endorsed for all parties on site, often at little or no cost. A leak-detection and automatic shut-off system on the temporary water supply, perhaps 30,000 dollars. Against roughly 2,600,000 dollars of uninsured repair and 1,200,000 dollars of uninsured delay, the trade was never close.

The prevention rule

Rule 79: Never accept insurance or bonds on a certificate alone; read the wording for limits, sublimits, exclusions, named insureds, waivers of subrogation, notice conditions and expiry, and keep every policy and bond in a register checked monthly until the last obligation ends.

Professional sign-off required: insurance broker acting for the owner, on the programme and the wordings; lawyer, on the insurance clauses in the contract.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a mismatch between the contract's allocation and the insurance behind it: a risk the contract gives to the contractor, insured under a policy that excludes it or sublimits it to a fraction of the exposure. The control is to give your broker the contract's risk clauses and ask, in writing, whether the proposed policies match them.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks the headline limit and stops. Sublimits, deductibles, exclusions and named insureds decide what a policy pays. Read the schedule of sublimits first.

Callback

In Week 53, Duke taught that safety is designed and supervised, not hoped for. Water damage during construction is the same: a temporary water system needs isolation valves, leak detection and an out-of-hours watch, just as an excavation needs shoring. The cheapest insurance claim is the one prevented on site.

Recap

A pipe joint failed on a weekend and flooded five floors. The policy had a water sublimit, did not name the owner, had no delay cover and no waiver of subrogation, so the insurer paid a fraction, sued the subcontractor and the parties fought while repairs waited. The owner carried most of the repair and all of the delay. Rule 79 makes the wording, not the certificate, the test.

Next: Priya on The Money: what insurance, bonds and letters of credit cost, and how they change the budget and the loan.
checklist: I obtain and read the full policy wording before work starts, not only the certificate.
I check the schedule of sublimits, especially water, and the deductibles.
I confirm that my company and my lender are named insureds or loss payees.
I decide deliberately whether to buy delay in start-up cover, with a number in front of me.
I require a waiver of subrogation among the parties on site.
I give my broker the contract's risk clauses and ask in writing whether the policies match.
I require leak detection, isolation and an out-of-hours watch on temporary water systems.

terms: Sublimit — a lower limit inside a policy that caps what it pays for one type of loss, whatever the headline limit.
Subrogation — the insurer's right, after paying a claim, to step into the insured's position and sue whoever caused the loss.
Named insured — a party listed on a policy with its own right to claim under it.

hostile.q: Your building is five months late after a water loss. Why should your investors not treat this as a failure of management?
hostile.a: Part of it was. We accepted the contractor's certificate without reading the wording, and we did not buy delay cover. I am telling you that plainly. Here is what we have changed: an owner's broker now reviews every wording against the contract, the owner and lender are named on all project policies, we have bought delay in start-up cover for the remaining work, and the site has leak detection and weekend monitoring. Here is the revised schedule and its effect on returns.

title: What Protection Costs, and Who Really Pays for It
summary: Insurance premiums, bond premiums and letters of credit all end up in the owner's cost, either directly or inside the contractor's price. Choosing a deductible is a self-insurance decision you can price with expected value. And a letter of credit is cheap on paper but expensive in the contractor's borrowing capacity.
body:
Every form of protection on a project ends up in the owner's cost, whoever buys it. The money skill is to see each one as a price for transferring a defined risk, and to decide how much risk you would rather keep and fund yourself.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 79?

A. Never accept insurance or bonds on a certificate alone; read the wording for limits, sublimits, exclusions, named insureds, waivers of subrogation, notice conditions and expiry, and keep a register checked monthly.

Q. In Week 77, what does a notice provision usually demand, and how does that connect to insurance?

A. Written notice to a named person, in a set form, within a set time. Insurance policies have the same kind of condition, so a late or informal notice to an insurer can put a claim at risk.

Q. In Week 71, why does consistent investor reporting protect the sponsor?

A. Because a record of honest, timely reports shows investors were told the truth as events unfolded, which is the best defence against a later claim that something material was hidden.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, insurance and bonds are often a line in the budget nobody questions. On a mid-size project they can add up to a meaningful share of hard cost, and the choices inside them, the deductible, who buys the builder's risk, whether to take a bond or a letter of credit, move real money. All figures today are hypothetical round numbers. Premium rates are set by the market for each risk and change with conditions; treat every rate below as an illustration, not a benchmark.

Where the cost sits

In plain English: if the contractor buys the protection, you still pay for it, inside its price, usually with a markup.

Take a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar construction contract. Suppose builder's risk costs about 0.3 percent of the insured value, 60,000 dollars; the contractor's general liability attributable to the job is 100,000 dollars; and a performance and payment bond costs about 1 percent of the contract, 200,000 dollars. That is 360,000 dollars of protection. If the contractor buys all of it and adds its fee of, say, 5 percent, you pay 378,000 dollars. None of that is waste, but all of it is a choice.

The professional framing is the question of who controls the programme. When the owner buys key policies, it chooses the insurer, the limits and the wording, and sees every claim. When the contractor buys them, it chooses, and the owner's protection depends on what it bought. On larger projects owners sometimes buy a wrap-up programme: an owner-controlled insurance programme (OCIP), or a contractor-controlled one (CCIP), covering everyone on site under one set of policies. A wrap-up can lower total cost through bulk buying and fewer gaps between policies, but it needs administration, enrolment of every subcontractor and close control of who is in and out. Whether it pays depends on project size and the local market, and it is commercial practice, not a standard.

The deductible is self-insurance

In plain English: a deductible is the part of every loss you agree to pay yourself, in exchange for a lower premium.

A worked example, hypothetical. Your broker offers builder's risk with a 25,000 dollar deductible for a premium of 80,000 dollars, or a 250,000 dollar deductible for 50,000 dollars. The higher deductible saves 30,000 dollars. Is it worth it?

Estimate losses. Your broker's view, from the project type and site, is a 40 percent chance of one claim of around 100,000 dollars and a 10 percent chance of one large claim of around 1,000,000 dollars over the build. Under the low deductible, you pay 25,000 dollars per claim: expected cost 0.4 times 25,000 plus 0.1 times 25,000, which is 12,500 dollars. Under the high deductible, the 100,000 dollar claim is below the deductible, so you pay all of it, and you pay 250,000 dollars of the large one: expected cost 0.4 times 100,000 plus 0.1 times 250,000, which is 65,000 dollars. The extra expected cost of the high deductible is 52,500 dollars, more than the 30,000 dollar premium saving. Keep the low deductible.

Change one input and the answer can flip. If the broker judges small claims much less likely, the high deductible may win. That is the point of doing the arithmetic: the right deductible depends on the loss pattern, and on whether you have the cash to fund the deductible when a loss arrives.

Say that out loud now.

A deductible is risk I keep. I price it with expected value and fund it with cash.

Bond or letter of credit: the hidden cost

Owners often prefer a letter of credit to a bond, because a bank pays on demand while a surety investigates. The cost is less visible.

A second worked example, hypothetical. You ask for a letter of credit of 10 percent of the 20,000,000 dollar contract, 2,000,000 dollars. The contractor's bank charges a fee, say 1.5 percent a year, 30,000 dollars a year, over two years 60,000 dollars. More importantly, the bank counts the 2,000,000 dollars against the contractor's credit line, or demands cash collateral. A contractor with a 5,000,000 dollar line has just lost 40 percent of its working capital for your job. It will price that, it may bid fewer jobs, and it may be less able to survive a cash squeeze, which is the very failure you were protecting against. A performance bond of 50 percent, 10,000,000 dollars, may cost the contractor about the same in premium, gives the owner a surety obliged to address completion, and leaves the contractor's bank line intact. Neither instrument is always better. Decide by asking what failure you fear most, and which instrument actually solves it.

What the lender requires

Construction lenders specify the insurance and bonds they need in the commitment letter: types of cover, minimum limits, that the lender is named as loss payee on property policies and additional insured on liability, and often that the lender approves the insurers. Bonds may be required with the lender named as a dual obligee, so it can claim directly. These requirements are commercial practice and vary by lender. Missing them is a condition precedent failure that can stop the first draw, so give your broker the commitment letter early.

The Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Every deductible and every uninsured risk your project keeps is self-insurance, and self-insurance needs cash. If a large deductible or an uninsured delay could require you to inject equity personally, that call on your liquidity belongs in your personal planning beside the guarantees from Week 40. The same logic applies at home: a higher deductible on your own policies is only sensible if your liquidity floor can absorb it without strain. Week 88 returns to insurance architecture for your personal life. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing protection by premium alone: the cheapest policy, the highest deductible or the instrument that looks tough on paper, without asking what it pays, when, and whether you can fund the part you keep. The control is expected-value pricing of the deductible, a cash plan for the retained risk, and a clear statement of which failure each instrument is meant to cover.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a letter of credit is free because the contractor pays the bank fee. It is in the bid, and it weakens the contractor's balance sheet at the same time.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught sources and uses and the four cost buckets: land, hard, soft and finance. Insurance and bonds sit across those buckets, some inside the contractor's hard cost, some in the owner's soft cost. Track them as one line in your own analysis, so you can see the whole price of protection in one place.

Recap

Protection always ends up in the owner's cost. Decide who controls the programme. Price the deductible as self-insurance with expected value and fund it with cash. Weigh a letter of credit's speed against its hidden cost to the contractor. Give the broker the lender's requirements early.

Next: LEX on The Rules: how insurance and surety law read notice, disclosure, subrogation and changes to the contract, with a comparison of two systems.
checklist: I can state the total cost of protection on the project, wherever it sits in the budget.
I have decided deliberately who controls the main policies.
I have priced the deductible options with expected value, using my broker's loss view.
I have cash set aside for the deductibles and uninsured risks I keep.
I know what a letter of credit would do to the contractor's working capital.
I can say which failure each bond or letter of credit is meant to cover.
My broker has the lender's insurance requirements before the commitment is signed.

A deductible is self-insurance. If the low deductible of 25,000 dollars costs 30,000 more in premium but the high deductible of 250,000 adds 52,500 dollars of expected cost, I keep the low one. The answer depends on the loss pattern and on whether I have the cash to pay the part I keep. Rates are market practice, not standards.
terms: Deductible — the amount of each loss the insured pays before the policy responds; a form of self-insurance.
Wrap-up programme — a single insurance programme, owner-controlled (OCIP) or contractor-controlled (CCIP), covering all parties on a site.
Loss payee — a party, such as a lender, named on a property policy to receive claim payments.

hostile.q: You chose the low deductible and paid 30,000 dollars more in premium. Why waste money?
hostile.a: I compared it with the expected cost of the losses I would keep. On the broker's loss view, the high deductible adds about 52,500 dollars of expected cost, more than the premium saving, and it would need cash I would rather keep in contingency. If you have a different loss view, show me, and I will re-run it. I am not buying the most insurance; I am buying the cheapest total cost of risk.

title: The Rules That Decide Whether a Policy or a Bond Pays
summary: Insurance and surety are contracts with their own legal rules. Insurance turns on disclosure, notice and how a policy is triggered; subrogation decides who the insurer can sue afterwards. Surety turns on conditions to claim and on the old rule that changing the guaranteed contract without consent can release the surety. A comparison of two systems closes the lesson.
body:
A policy or a bond pays only if you have kept its conditions. Insurance law turns on disclosure, notice and trigger; surety law turns on conditions to claim and on not changing the contract behind the surety's back.

Recall

Q. Why is a deductible a form of self-insurance?

A. Because it is the part of each loss the insured agrees to pay itself, in exchange for a lower premium, so it must be priced with expected value and funded with cash.

Q. In Week 77, what does a condition precedent do?

A. It makes an entitlement depend on a step being taken first, such as notice in a stated form and time. If the step is missed, the entitlement may never arise.

Q. In Week 71, what is the general measure of a misrepresentation claim?

A. Whether a statement of material fact was false or misleading, or an omission made the rest misleading, and whether the investor relied on it or was entitled to rely on it under the applicable law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an owner who has read the wording of every policy can still lose the claim by sending notice late, by failing to disclose a known problem when the policy was bought, or by agreeing a major change with the contractor without telling the surety. These are general common-law concepts. The rules vary between jurisdictions and are often changed by statute; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Insurance: disclosure, notice and trigger

In plain English: tell the insurer the truth when you buy, tell it promptly when something happens, and know what event switches the policy on.

Disclosure first. In the common-law tradition, insurance contracts were treated as contracts of utmost good faith: the person buying cover had to disclose every fact material to the insurer's decision, whether or not asked, and serious non-disclosure could let the insurer avoid the policy. Several jurisdictions have since moderated this rule by statute, shifting more of the burden onto insurers to ask questions [unverified — confirm independently]. The safe practice is unchanged: if you know about a ground problem, a previous water loss or a dispute with a subcontractor, disclose it in writing when the cover is placed.

Notice second. Most policies require notice of a loss or claim as soon as practicable, and many require cooperation and no admission of liability without the insurer's consent. Some courts treat a late notice as fatal only if it prejudiced the insurer; others treat the condition strictly. Send written notice the day you know, even if you are not yet sure there is a claim.

Trigger third. An occurrence policy responds to events that happen during the policy period, whenever the claim is made. A claims-made policy, common for professional indemnity, responds to claims first made during the policy period, so the policy in force when the claim arrives is the one that matters, which is why run-off cover after completion is essential for designers.

A worked example, hypothetical. A consultant designs a building in years 1 and 2 under a claims-made policy, then lets the policy lapse in year 4. In year 6, a defect appears and you claim. There is no policy in force to respond. If the appointment had required the consultant to keep cover in force for, say, six years after completion, the claim would meet a live policy. The length of that period, and the limitation period for the claim itself, are set by contract and by local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Subrogation and how to switch it off

After paying a claim, an insurer is usually subrogated: it may sue whoever caused the loss, in the insured's name. On a construction site that can set the insurer of one party against another party on the same project, as in the Day 2 case. A waiver of subrogation is a contract term in which the parties give up claims against each other for losses covered by insurance. For it to work, it usually needs two things: the clause in the construction contract, and the insurer's agreement, often by endorsement, since a policy may be breached if the insured gives away the insurer's recovery rights without permission. Naming all the main parties as insureds on one property policy can achieve the same end, because an insurer generally cannot sue its own insured.

Say that out loud now.

A waiver of subrogation needs the contract clause and the insurer's consent, or it may not hold.

Surety: conditions and the material variation rule

A surety's obligation is secondary: it answers for the contractor's default, not instead of it. Two rules follow.

First, conditions to claim. Many performance bonds require the owner to declare the contractor in default, give written notice to the surety, and keep the remaining contract balance available for completion, before the surety must act. Pay that balance to someone else, or skip the formal declaration, and the surety may argue it is released. Read the bond's claim procedure before the first sign of trouble, not after.

Second, the material variation rule. An old common-law principle, associated with the English case of Holme v Brunskill in 1878, holds that a guarantor can be discharged if the guaranteed contract is varied in a way that could prejudice it, without its consent. Modern bonds usually contain wording permitting changes, extensions of time and indulgences without releasing the surety, but the protection is only as good as that wording. A large change in scope, an advance payment not anticipated by the contract, or a big extension of time can all raise the question.

A second worked example, hypothetical. On a 15,000,000 dollar contract with a 7,500,000 dollar performance bond, the owner agrees to add a podium car park worth 4,000,000 dollars and to advance the contractor 1,000,000 dollars to buy steel early. Nobody tells the surety. Six months later the contractor fails. The surety argues that the change and the unsecured advance increased its risk without consent. Even if the bond's variation wording defeats that argument, the owner now has a dispute with the party it was relying on. A one-page letter to the surety, seeking consent to the change and the advance, would have cost nothing.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach these points. Verify against primary source before relying on any of it.

Canada. Insurance and much of construction law are provincial matters, so the rules on disclosure, notice and statutory conditions in policies differ between provinces, and Quebec applies its civil code, with its own provisions on insurance and suretyship, rather than common law [unverified — confirm independently]. Bonds are widely used on public and large private work, and industry bodies publish standard bond and contract forms that owners often adopt. Provincial lien and prompt payment legislation interacts with payment bonds, because both protect subcontractors [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana. The legal system follows the English common-law tradition for contract, so concepts such as utmost good faith, subrogation and the surety's secondary liability are likely to be approached in a similar way, while insurers are regulated under the country's own insurance legislation by its financial regulator [unverified — confirm independently]. Public procurement rules commonly require bid security and performance security from contractors on public contracts, often as a bond or bank guarantee [unverified — confirm independently]. On a private project, what is required, and in what form, is largely for the contract to say.

The lesson across both: the instrument's wording and the local statute together decide whether it pays. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, in the governing jurisdiction, on the policies and bonds; insurance broker licensed in that jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is losing cover you paid for by breaking a condition: non-disclosure at placement, late notice, a waiver of subrogation without insurer consent, or a contract change without the surety's consent. The control is a written procedure: disclose in writing, notify the same day, get endorsements, and write to the surety before any material change or advance.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner waits until a loss is certain before notifying the insurer, to avoid a fuss. Notify on suspicion. A notice that turns out to be unnecessary costs nothing; a late one can cost the claim.

Callback

In Week 39, Priya taught conditions precedent in a loan: steps that must happen before the lender has to fund. Insurance policies and bonds work the same way. Each has its own conditions, and the money moves only when they are met.

Recap

Disclose material facts when cover is placed, notify losses on suspicion, and know whether a policy is triggered by occurrence or by claim. Make a waiver of subrogation work with both the contract clause and the insurer's consent. Follow the bond's claim procedure exactly, and get the surety's consent before material changes or advances. Local statute can change all of it.

Next: Priya on The Numbers: what a performance bond actually recovers when a contractor defaults.
checklist: I disclose known problems to insurers in writing when cover is placed.
I notify insurers in writing on suspicion of a loss, the same day I learn of it.
I know which policies are occurrence-based and which are claims-made.
I require consultants to keep claims-made cover in force for a stated period after completion.
Every waiver of subrogation is backed by the insurer's endorsement.
I have read the claim procedure in every performance bond.
I write to the surety before any material change, extension or advance payment.
Counsel in the governing jurisdiction has reviewed the policies and bonds.
head: Field checklist
speak: A policy or a bond pays only if I keep its conditions. For insurance, that means three things. Disclosure: the common law treated insurance as utmost good faith, so I disclose known problems in writing when cover is placed, even where statutes have softened the rule. Notice: I notify on suspicion, the same day, because late notice can cost the claim. Trigger: occurrence policies answer for events in the period, claims-made policies for claims made in the period, so designers must keep cover in force after completion. Subrogation lets an insurer sue whoever caused a loss, and a waiver only holds with the contract clause and the insurer's endorsement. For surety, I follow the bond's claim procedure exactly, declaring default and keeping the contract balance available, and I get the surety's consent before a material change or advance, because the old material variation rule can release a guarantor. Canada and Guyana differ in statute, so counsel checks.
terms: Utmost good faith — the traditional common-law rule that a person buying insurance must disclose all material facts, whether asked or not.
Claims-made policy — a policy that responds to claims first made during the policy period, regardless of when the work was done.
Material variation rule — the principle that a guarantor can be released if the guaranteed contract is changed to its prejudice without its consent.

hostile.q: You changed the contract and advanced 1,000,000 dollars to the contractor without telling us. Why should the surety still answer for this default?
hostile.a: I would rather not argue that point, because you may have a case and the bond's variation wording may defeat it. What I can show you is the change order and the advance, both documented, the security we took for the advance, and that the remaining contract balance is intact and available for completion. Let us agree the completion route first and take the release argument separately, so the building is not hostage to it.

title: What a Performance Bond Actually Recovers
summary: A worked calculation of a contractor default, step by step: the unpaid contract balance, the cost to complete, the owner's extra costs, what the performance bond covers, what the payment bond covers, and how a letter of credit would have compared. Hypothetical round numbers throughout.
body:
A performance bond does not pay you its penal sum. It pays, at most, the gap between what it costs to finish and what you still owed the failed contractor. Learn to calculate that gap before the default, and you know what your bond is really worth.

Recall

Q. What is the material variation rule?

A. The principle that a guarantor, such as a surety, can be released if the guaranteed contract is changed to its prejudice without its consent. Modern bonds usually limit it by express wording.

Q. In Week 77, what is a schedule of values, and why does it matter after a default?

A. The contractor's list of budget lines its payment applications are billed against. After a default it shows what has been paid for, line by line, which is the starting point for working out what remains.

Q. In Week 71, why must an offering document describe material risks specifically?

A. Because generic warnings do not tell investors what could actually happen to this project, and a risk that was known but described only in boilerplate can support a later claim that it was not properly disclosed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a contractor fails, you have perhaps a week to decide how to finish your building, and the surety will take longer than that to decide what it owes. If you already know the arithmetic, you can make the surety's decision easy and fast, and you can see whether your protection was ever enough. All figures are hypothetical round numbers. Penal sums, retainage rates and premium rates are commercial practice and, on public work, sometimes set by rule; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Step 1: the set-up

A lump-sum contract of 12,000,000 dollars. A performance bond with a penal sum of 50 percent, 6,000,000 dollars, and a separate payment bond of the same amount. Retainage of 10 percent is held on every payment. The bond premium was about 1 percent of the contract, 120,000 dollars, inside the contractor's price.

In month 10, the contractor stops work. The lender's monitor and your cost consultant agree that work in place is worth 6,500,000 dollars, all of it certified and paid less retainage.

Step 2: what you still owed the contractor

  1. Certified to date: 6,500,000 dollars.
  2. Retainage held: 10 percent of 6,500,000, which is 650,000 dollars.
  3. Cash paid: 6,500,000 less 650,000, which is 5,850,000 dollars.
  4. Unpaid contract balance: 12,000,000 less 5,850,000, which is 6,150,000 dollars.

That 6,150,000 dollars, including the retainage, is the money you would have paid to finish the job if nothing had gone wrong. It is your first source of funds for completion, and most bonds expect you to keep it available for that purpose.

Track this number every month, not only at default. A contractor that bills ahead of the work, or an owner that releases retainage early, shrinks the unpaid balance while the real cost to complete stays where it was. The gap between the two is exactly what the surety will be asked to fill, so a shrinking balance means a larger claim on the bond and a larger chance of exceeding the penal sum. If retainage had been reduced to 5 percent halfway through, the balance here would have been 325,000 dollars smaller, and the excess 325,000 dollars larger.

Step 3: what it now costs to finish

You re-tender the remaining work.

ItemAmount
Replacement contractor's price to complete8,000,000 dollars
Correcting defective work found in the failed contractor's work300,000 dollars
Re-procurement, design and legal costs200,000 dollars
Cost to complete8,500,000 dollars

The replacement price is higher than the original contract rate because the new contractor is taking over someone else's half-built work, with its defects and missing records, in a hurry. That premium is normal.

Step 4: the performance bond's share

  1. Cost to complete: 8,500,000 dollars.
  2. Less the unpaid contract balance: 6,150,000 dollars.
  3. Excess cost: 2,350,000 dollars.
  4. Penal sum: 6,000,000 dollars, so the excess is within it.

The surety's obligation, subject to the bond wording and to your having met its conditions, covers the 2,350,000 dollar excess. It does not hand you 6,000,000 dollars. The penal sum is a ceiling, not a payment.

Say that out loud now.

The bond covers the gap between cost to complete and the balance I still owed, up to the penal sum.

Step 5: delay, the part that may not be covered

The default and re-tender cost 90 days. At the daily cost of delay from Week 78's model, about 8,000 dollars a day, that is 720,000 dollars of interest, fees and lost net rent. Some bond forms include the owner's delay damages or liquidated damages within the surety's obligation; others exclude them or leave them to argument. Read your bond. If it includes them, the surety's share rises to 3,070,000 dollars, still within the penal sum. If it excludes them, the 720,000 dollars is yours, to be pursued against the insolvent contractor's estate, which may pay little.

Step 6: the subcontractors and the payment bond

At default, unpaid subcontractors and suppliers are owed 400,000 dollars for work already in place. Without a payment bond, they may register liens against your property under local lien law, and the replacement subcontractors may refuse to start until they are settled. The payment bond is a separate obligation: subject to its claim conditions and notice periods, the surety pays those claimants. Your lender, who needs a clean title for the next draw, cares about this as much as you do.

Step 7: compare a letter of credit

Suppose instead the contract had required a letter of credit for 10 percent of the contract, 1,200,000 dollars, and no bond. You could draw it within days, which is fast. But it covers 1,200,000 dollars of a 2,350,000 dollar excess, leaving 1,150,000 dollars, plus the delay, plus the 400,000 dollars of subcontractor claims, with you. In this default, speed was worth less than size. On a different project, where the risk is a small defect or an unpaid warranty claim, the letter of credit's speed might matter more. The calculation tells you which.

Step 8: test the protection before you need it

Run this calculation at contract award, with a severe default case. If the excess in your severe case exceeds the penal sum, the bond is too small. If the uncovered delay is large, consider whether your contingency and equity can carry it. A second worked example, hypothetical: if the replacement price had been 11,000,000 dollars, the excess would have been 11,500,000 less 6,150,000, which is 5,350,000 dollars, still just inside the 6,000,000 dollar penal sum. At 12,500,000 dollars it would exceed it. Know where your line is.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the bond conditions and the default procedure; quantity surveyor, on work in place and cost to complete.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is destroying your own recovery by spending the unpaid balance. If you release retainage early, overpay the failed contractor, or pay the balance to others before the surety agrees the completion route, the surety may argue that its obligation shrank or ended. The control is to freeze payments on default, notify the surety in writing, and agree the completion route before money moves.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the penal sum as the amount the bond pays. It is the maximum; the real recovery is the excess cost over the balance you still owed.

Callback

In Week 40, the in-balance test asked whether undisbursed loan plus equity covered the cost to complete. A contractor default is that same test under stress: the unpaid contract balance plus the surety's share must cover the new cost to complete, or the gap lands on equity.

Recap

Calculate the unpaid balance, including retainage. Calculate the full cost to complete. The performance bond covers the excess, up to the penal sum, subject to its wording. Delay may or may not be covered. The payment bond protects subcontractors and your title. Compare a letter of credit's speed against its size, and run the test at award.

Next: Priya, with Marco, in The Room: the site meeting the morning after a loss, with the adjuster, the contractor and your broker.
checklist: At award, I calculate the bond's recovery in a severe default case.
I know the unpaid contract balance, including retainage, at every month end.
I know whether my bond covers delay damages or liquidated damages.
I hold retainage until completion and refuse early releases without surety consent.
On default, I freeze payments and notify the surety in writing the same day.
I agree the completion route with the surety before any balance is spent.
I check subcontractor claims against the payment bond's notice periods.
head: Field checklist
speak: A performance bond pays the gap, not its penal sum. On a 12,000,000 dollar contract, if the contractor fails after 6,500,000 dollars of certified work, I have paid 5,850,000 and held 650,000 retainage, so the unpaid balance is 6,150,000. If it costs 8,500,000 to finish, including defects and re-procurement, the excess is 2,350,000. That is what the surety covers, up to the 6,000,000 dollar penal sum, if I have met the bond's conditions. Delay of 90 days at 8,000 dollars a day, 720,000, may or may not be covered; the wording decides. The payment bond separately protects the 400,000 owed to subcontractors and keeps liens off my title. A 10 percent letter of credit would have paid 1,200,000 fast and left over a million uncovered. So I run this test at award, and on default I freeze payments, notify the surety and agree the route before any money moves.
terms: Penal sum — the maximum amount a surety can be required to pay under a bond.
Unpaid contract balance — the contract sum less cash already paid, including retainage held, available to fund completion after a default.
Payment bond — a bond guaranteeing that subcontractors and suppliers are paid, reducing liens on the owner's property.

hostile.q: Your contractor has failed. The surety wants six weeks to investigate. How do you keep the site going?
hostile.a: I have frozen payments and given the surety written notice, so its rights are protected. I am sharing our work-in-place survey, the unpaid balance of 6,150,000 dollars and a priced cost to complete, so its investigation can be short. Meanwhile I am securing the site and protecting the work from weather at my own cost, which I will claim. I am asking the surety for a decision on the completion route within two weeks, and I have a replacement contractor ready to price if it agrees.

title: The Site Meeting the Morning After a Loss
summary: A scene: a storm has torn off the temporary roofing and soaked three floors. The contractor, the insurer's loss adjuster and your broker are on site. You need to protect the work, preserve the claim and keep the project moving without admitting anything you should not. The lines to say, the lines never to say, and how to hold your state.
body:
The morning after a loss, your job is three things in this order: make the site safe and stop the damage getting worse, preserve the evidence and the claim, then restart the work. Everything you say in that meeting either helps one of those three or harms it.

Recall

Q. In Priya's calculation, what does a performance bond cover after a default?

A. The excess of the cost to complete over the unpaid contract balance, including retainage, up to the penal sum and subject to the bond's wording and conditions.

Q. In Week 77, what is an early warning provision?

A. A clause requiring a party to notify the other promptly of anything that could affect cost, time or quality, so both can act early. Some forms reduce the entitlement of a party that fails to warn.

Q. In Week 71, why should bad news reach investors as fast as good news?

A. Because delay makes a fair disclosure look like concealment, and because investors can only make decisions on information they have actually been given.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you have bought the right insurance and read the wordings. Now something has happened, and the first hours decide how much of that protection you actually collect. Insurers expect the insured to take reasonable steps to limit a loss, which professionals call mitigation. They expect prompt notice, cooperation and access. And they do not expect you to accept blame for the loss on the spot. Priya has done the money; I run the room. The numbers are hypothetical.

The scene

Your 30,000,000 dollar building is at month 14. Overnight a storm tore the temporary roofing off the top two floors, and water has run down through three floors of new drywall, insulation and electrical rough-in. Early estimate: 800,000 dollars of damage and perhaps six weeks of delay. It is 8 in the morning. On site: the contractor's project manager, defensive; the loss adjuster appointed by the builder's risk insurer, polite and careful; and your own broker, who arrived because you called at 6.

Before the meeting: what you have already done

At 6 you called the broker and sent written notice to the insurer through the broker, with photographs, the time you learned of the loss and the policy number. At 6.30 you told the contractor in writing to make the site safe, to cover exposed floors, to start drying and to keep every damaged item, not to throw anything away. At 7 you told your lender, briefly, that a weather loss had occurred and that you would send a fuller note within two days. Those three messages cost you twenty minutes and protect the whole claim.

The question behind the question

The adjuster's questions are about cause and condition. Was the temporary roofing installed and secured as it should have been? Was a weather warning issued and ignored? What damage existed before the storm? Behind them sits one question: is this a sudden insured event, or a failure of workmanship or maintenance that the policy may exclude? The contractor's question behind its silence is different: will this be blamed on us?

Your own question behind the question is the one that matters most: how fast can we be building again, and who funds the gap until the insurer pays?

The lines to say

To the adjuster. "Thank you for coming so quickly. You'll have full access. We've kept all damaged material, and here are the photographs from 6 this morning, the temporary works drawings and the weather records. Tell us what else you need, and we'll get it to you today."

On mitigation. "We are drying the floors and stripping wet drywall to stop mould. Is there anything you would like us to hold, or to record before it is removed?" Asking this first protects you from a later argument that removal destroyed evidence.

To the contractor. "Our priority is the same as yours: get this dry and get back to work. We'll deal with cause in the proper way, through the policy and the contract, not this morning."

To your broker, privately. "Walk me through the policy conditions that apply now: notice, mitigation, consent to repair, and whether delay cover responds."

Say that out loud now.

Safe first, evidence second, restart third. Blame later, in writing, through the right channel.

The lines never to say

Never say: "This is the contractor's fault; they never tied the roof down properly." You do not know that yet, you may be wrong, and it is the kind of statement an insurer can rely on to argue the loss was a workmanship failure. Many policies also forbid admissions of liability without the insurer's consent.

Never say: "Just fix it and send me the bill." Many policies require the insurer's agreement before permanent repairs, beyond emergency work. Repairs begun without it can be disputed.

Never say to the adjuster: "We're fully covered for this, aren't we?" It tells the adjuster you have not read your own policy and invites a careful answer that commits the insurer to nothing.

When to stay silent

When the adjuster and the contractor begin discussing how the roofing was secured, stay out of it. That is a factual question for the people who did the work, and your speculation helps nobody. Listen, take notes and ask afterwards for the contractor's written account.

Stay silent, too, after you ask the adjuster for a timeline on accepting the claim. Let the answer come. If you fill the gap, you will soften your own request.

Holding your state

Losses produce a surge of adrenaline and a strong urge to act and to blame. Week 4's lesson holds: name the feeling to yourself, slow your speech, and keep your hands still. If you need it, take a few slow breaths in your parked car before you walk on site, not while driving. A calm owner signals to every party that the project is under control, and that changes how the adjuster, the contractor and the lender treat the next six weeks.

After the meeting: the money

A worked example, hypothetical. Damage of 800,000 dollars, less a 50,000 dollar deductible, gives an insured repair of 750,000 dollars if the claim is accepted. Six weeks of delay at the 8,000 dollar daily cost from Week 78 is about 336,000 dollars, covered only if you bought delay in start-up cover, and then only after its own waiting period. Until the insurer pays, the contractor needs funding to keep crews on site. A second worked example: if the insurer agrees an interim payment of 300,000 dollars within three weeks, and your contingency carries the rest of the repair cash flow for another five weeks, you avoid demobilising the drywall crew, which could otherwise add two weeks and 112,000 dollars of delay. Ask for an interim payment early; adjusters often agree to them for undisputed parts of a claim.

Professional sign-off required: insurance broker, on the claim; lawyer, if the insurer reserves its rights or the contractor disputes cause.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is losing part of an insured claim in the first day: by a careless admission, by throwing away damaged material before the adjuster sees it, or by starting permanent repairs without the insurer's agreement. The control is the morning routine: notice, photographs, preserve, mitigate, and ask before you remove or repair.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads the meeting with blame. Lead with safety and access. Cause is decided later, from evidence, under the policy and the contract.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the commitment to confirm by a date. The morning after a loss is that pattern under pressure. Acknowledge the damage, bridge to what has been done, answer with what happens next and by when.

Recap

Before the meeting: notice, photographs, preserve and tell the lender. In the meeting: give access, ask before removing anything, keep cause out of the conversation. Never admit fault, never start permanent repairs without agreement, never ask if you are covered. Hold your state, ask for an interim payment, and fund the gap from contingency so the site keeps moving.

Next: Kema on the Week 79 review: six questions, a Red Pen drill on an insurance clause and a certificate, and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I notify the insurer in writing through the broker the morning I learn of a loss.
I photograph the damage and tell the contractor in writing to keep all damaged material.
I tell the lender promptly and briefly, with a fuller note to follow.
I ask the adjuster before anything is removed or permanently repaired.
I make no statement about cause or fault at the site meeting.
I ask early for an interim payment on the undisputed part of the claim.
I fund the gap from contingency to avoid demobilising crews.
head: Field checklist
speak: The morning after a loss I do three things in order: make the site safe and stop the damage spreading, preserve the evidence and the claim, then restart the work. Before the meeting I have sent written notice to the insurer through my broker, taken photographs, told the contractor in writing to keep every damaged item, and told my lender briefly. In the meeting I give the adjuster full access and ask what to hold or record before anything is removed. I keep cause out of the conversation, because an admission can help an insurer argue the loss was a workmanship failure. I never say just fix it, because permanent repairs may need the insurer's agreement, and I never ask whether we are covered. I hold my state and speak slowly. Then I ask for an interim payment on the undisputed part, and fund the gap from contingency so the crews stay on site.
terms: Mitigation — reasonable steps taken by the insured to stop a loss growing, which most policies require.
Loss adjuster — a professional appointed, usually by the insurer, to investigate a claim's cause and value.
Interim payment — part payment of an insurance claim before the whole claim is settled, usually for the undisputed portion.

hostile.q: The adjuster says the temporary roof was not secured to the manufacturer's instructions and the loss may be excluded. What do you do?
hostile.a: I do not argue the point on site. I ask the adjuster to set out the position in writing and which exclusion is relied on, and I give my broker the policy wording and the temporary works records. If there was a workmanship failure, the policy may still cover the resulting damage even if it excludes the defective part, depending on its wording, and the contract may make the contractor responsible for what is not covered. Meanwhile we keep drying and protecting the building, because mitigation is required whatever the answer.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 79 Review: The Promises Behind the Contract
summary: Six questions test the week: insurance against surety, Rule 79, the deductible as self-insurance, disclosure, notice and subrogation, what a performance bond recovers, and the morning after a loss. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical insurance clause and certificate, then a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: insurance and surety make a risk allocation collectable, but only if you have read the wording, kept the conditions and know which instrument answers which event.

Recall

Q. What is mitigation, in the context of an insurance claim?

A. The reasonable steps the insured takes to stop a loss growing, such as covering and drying a soaked building. Most policies require it.

Q. In Week 77, why does the order of the contract documents matter when an insurance requirement appears in two places?

A. Because if the conditions and the specification state different limits or covers, the order of precedence decides which one binds the contractor.

Q. In Week 71, what does a fiduciary owe when its own interest conflicts with the investor's?

A. Disclosure of the conflict and, depending on the relationship and the law, either the investor's informed consent or putting the investor's interest first.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can sit with a broker, a surety and a lender and know whether the protection on your project is real. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the decisive difference between insurance and a surety bond?

Answer: Insurance pools accidental losses and expects to pay claims. A surety guarantees a contractor's promise, underwrites the contractor and expects to be repaid by it under an indemnity.

Question 2. State Rule 79.

Answer: Never accept insurance or bonds on a certificate alone; read the wording for limits, sublimits, exclusions, named insureds, waivers of subrogation, notice conditions and expiry, and keep every policy and bond in a register checked monthly until the last obligation ends.

Question 3. How do you choose a deductible?

Answer: Treat it as self-insurance. Compare the premium saving with the extra expected cost of the losses you would keep, using the broker's loss view, and confirm you have the cash to fund the deductible when a loss arrives.

Question 4. What does a waiver of subrogation do, and what does it need to work?

Answer: It stops an insurer that has paid a claim from suing other parties on the project. It usually needs both the clause in the construction contract and the insurer's agreement, often by endorsement.

Question 5. A 12,000,000 dollar contract fails with an unpaid balance of 6,150,000 dollars and a cost to complete of 8,500,000 dollars. The penal sum is 6,000,000 dollars. What does the performance bond cover?

Answer: The excess, 2,350,000 dollars, within the penal sum, subject to the bond's wording and conditions. Delay damages are covered only if the bond includes them.

Question 6. What three things do you do, in order, the morning after a loss?

Answer: Make the site safe and stop the damage spreading, preserve the evidence and the claim with notice, photographs and kept material, then restart the work, asking the insurer before permanent repairs.

Say that out loud now.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical insurance clause and the certificate supplied under it. Find the defects before reading on.

Clause 22. The Contractor shall maintain builder's risk insurance for the value of the Works and general liability insurance of 2,000,000 dollars, and shall provide certificates on request. The Contractor shall provide a performance bond of 10 percent. Certificate attached: Insured — ABC Construction Ltd. Builder's risk — limit 25,000,000 dollars. General liability — 2,000,000 dollars aggregate. Policy period — to 31 March. Terms and conditions as per policy.

The defects. First, builder's risk for the value of the works does not say whether that is the contract sum or the full replacement value including owner-supplied items and design fees, or whether it rises as changes are added. Second, the owner and its lender are not required to be named insureds or loss payees, and the certificate shows only the contractor. Third, there is no requirement for a waiver of subrogation, or for the insurer's endorsement of one. Fourth, certificates are provided only on request, not before work starts and at each renewal, so a lapse could go unnoticed. Fifth, the certificate shows a policy period ending 31 March with no year and no renewal obligation, while the works will plainly run beyond it. Sixth, the general liability limit is aggregate only, so other claims against the contractor elsewhere could erode it. Seventh, the performance bond is 10 percent with no payment bond at all, no stated surety standard and no named obligee, which on the Day 5 numbers would have covered well under half of a realistic default. And the certificate's last line, terms and conditions as per policy, is the signal that only the wording will tell you what is covered: sublimits, deductibles and exclusions are all missing.

Then the fix list. State the insured value as full replacement value, adjusted for changes. Name the owner and lender. Require waivers with endorsements. Require certificates and wordings before mobilisation and at every renewal, with notice of cancellation. Set per-occurrence and aggregate limits. Require performance and payment bonds with stated penal sums, from an acceptable surety, with the owner and lender as obligees.

The boardroom drill

Stand up and explain this week to an investment committee in two minutes. Start a timer.

Model answer: "Our contracts allocate risk; our insurance and bonds make that allocation collectable. We control the builder's risk policy ourselves, at full replacement value, with us and the lender named, a waiver of subrogation endorsed for everyone on site, and delay cover so a major loss does not become an uninsured interest bill. Every policy wording, not just the certificate, has been reviewed by our broker against the contract. Our deductible was chosen on expected cost, and contingency holds the cash to pay it. The contractor provides performance and payment bonds at 50 percent each. We have run a severe default case: the bond covers the excess cost to complete within its penal sum, and the payment bond protects our title from subcontractor liens. Everything sits in a register our project manager checks monthly, and we have a written routine for the first morning after any loss."

Score your answer. Did you separate insurance from surety? Did you name the wording review? Did you mention a tested default case? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is protection that exists on paper and fails in fact: a sublimit, a missing named insured, a lapsed policy, a late notice or a surety released by an unnotified change. The control is the register, the wording review and the written loss routine.

The beginner's mistake

Collecting certificates as if they were the protection. A certificate is a pointer to a promise; the wording is the promise.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman taught political-risk insurance for currency and expropriation risk abroad. The same discipline applies here, at a smaller scale: decide which risks the market can carry for you, read exactly what it promises, and keep the conditions that keep the promise alive.

Recap

Insurance pools accidents; surety guarantees promises. Read wordings, not certificates. Price the deductible as self-insurance. Disclose, notify on suspicion, endorse waivers and consult the surety before changes. Calculate what a bond really recovers. Run a calm, written routine the morning after a loss. Rule 79 makes the wording the test.

head: The six questions
speak: Insurance and surety make a risk allocation collectable. Insurance pools accidents and pays what its wording covers, less the deductible. A surety guarantees the contractor's promise and is repaid by the contractor. Rule 79: never accept insurance or bonds on a certificate alone; I read the wording for limits, sublimits, exclusions, named insureds, waivers and expiry, and keep a monthly register. A deductible is self-insurance, priced with expected value and funded with cash. I disclose known problems, notify on suspicion, and back every waiver of subrogation with the insurer's endorsement. I write to the surety before any material change. A performance bond covers the excess of cost to complete over the unpaid balance, up to the penal sum, so I test that at award. And the morning after a loss, I make the site safe, preserve the evidence and the claim, then restart, without admitting fault or starting permanent repairs unagreed.
terms: Certificate of insurance — a summary confirming a policy exists, which does not itself set out what the policy covers.
Full replacement value — the cost of rebuilding the insured works new, including design, owner-supplied items and changes.
Notice of cancellation — a requirement that the insurer or contractor tell the owner before a policy is cancelled or not renewed.

hostile.q: You have a certificate showing 25,000,000 dollars of builder's risk. Why do you need to see the policy?
hostile.a: Because the certificate does not show the water sublimit, the deductible, the exclusions, whether we and the lender are named, whether a waiver of subrogation is endorsed, or whether the policy renews before the job ends. Any one of those can make a 25,000,000 dollar headline worth a fraction of that on the day. We review the wording once, before mobilisation, and at each renewal. It takes our broker a day and protects the whole project.
